title: Threat Modeling with STRIDE
oneLiner: Draw what the system does, then ask six questions of every part of it: can someone spoof it, tamper with it, deny it, read it, stop it, or gain power through it?
keyTakeaway: Threat modeling is asking "what could go wrong?" while the design is still cheap to change. Draw a data flow diagram with trust boundaries, then walk each element through STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege. Every threat you find should end in a mitigation, an accepted risk, or a question to answer.
explanation:
Threat modeling is a structured way to find security problems in a design before they become problems in code. It answers four questions, popularized by Adam Shostack: What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good job? It needs no special tools, just a whiteboard and the people who know the system, and it's the main defence against Insecure Design in the OWASP Top 10, where the flaw is in the plan rather than the code.

Start with a data flow diagram (DFD): external entities (people and systems you don't control), processes (your code), data stores (databases, files) and the data flows between them. Then draw trust boundaries, the lines where data passes between areas trusted to different degrees, such as the internet and your web app, or the office network and the plant network. Threats cluster at those crossings.

STRIDE, created at Microsoft, gives six categories to ask about, each the opposite of a security property. Spoofing (pretending to be someone or something) breaks authentication. Tampering (changing data or code) breaks integrity. Repudiation (denying you did something, with no proof either way) breaks non-repudiation, which is why audit logs matter. Information disclosure breaks confidentiality. Denial of service breaks availability. Elevation of privilege (gaining rights you shouldn't have) breaks authorization. Not every category applies to every element: processes can suffer all six, data flows and data stores mostly tampering, disclosure and denial of service, and external entities spoofing and repudiation.
